skill: Status epilepticus refractory to first benzodiazepine
stem: A 55-year-old with epilepsy has ongoing generalised convulsion after 6 minutes. He received a correctly dosed IV lorazepam, but the seizure continues four minutes later. Airway support is underway and bedside glucose is normal.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate next intervention?
options: Stop all anticonvulsants and wait for 30 minutes because postictal movements can persist.
Repeat benzodiazepine in an appropriate protocol dose and promptly progress to second-line IV antiseizure loading if seizure persists.
Start oral maintenance valproate tablets without stopping the seizure.
Send to CT unmonitored before further treatment.
Perform lumbar puncture immediately to exclude encephalitis.
explanations: This is ongoing convulsive status, not postictal motion; delay risks cerebral injury.
Correct: established status follows a structured timed escalation while maintaining airway and circulation.
Oral maintenance therapy cannot reliably stop ongoing convulsions.
Moving an actively seizing patient without stabilisation can be dangerous.
Diagnostic workup must not delay seizure termination and airway support.
pearl: Treat ongoing convulsions by a time-based algorithm: early benzodiazepine, then a second-line loading drug, then anaesthetic critical care if refractory.
pivot: A brief self-terminating seizure without persistent altered consciousness may be assessed without immediate repeated loading doses.

steps: Stabilise
ABCDE, oxygen/ventilation, cardiac monitoring, glucose, IV/IO and timed seizure observations.
Escalate antiseizure therapy
Protocol repeat benzodiazepine if appropriate; second-line levetiracetam, valproate or fosphenytoin according to risks.
Investigate cause
Electrolytes, drug levels, infection, toxins, neuroimaging when stable.
Critical care
Anaesthetic therapy/intubation with EEG when refractory.
management.safety: Prevent respiratory depression with airway preparedness and avoid exceeding repeated benzodiazepine limits.
management.local: Educational answer; confirm local clinical guidelines, doses and relevant senior-led escalation.

skill: Acute upper GI bleed / transfusion strategy
stem: A 72-year-old presents with coffee-ground vomiting and melaena. BP is 94/58 mmHg, HR 112/min and Hb 64 g/L. She has severe ischaemic heart disease. There is no known portal hypertension.
ask: Which is the BEST immediate strategy?
options: Give IV PPI only and recheck haemoglobin tomorrow.
Order colonoscopy as the first procedure because stool is black.
Resuscitate, crossmatch and transfuse appropriately, start IV acid suppression and arrange urgent upper endoscopy.
Give high-dose aspirin for cardiovascular protection immediately despite ongoing haematemesis.
Routine prophylactic antibiotics and terlipressin for every upper GI bleed regardless of cause.
explanations: Significant blood loss with haemodynamic concern requires resuscitation and early endoscopy.
Melaena with haematemesis suggests upper GI source; upper endoscopy is prioritised.
Correct: stabilise and treat suspected high-risk ulcer bleed with targeted endoscopic haemostasis.
Antiplatelet balance must be specialist-reviewed in active life-threatening bleeding.
Vasoactive therapy/antibiotic prophylaxis is targeted to suspected variceal bleeding, not universal UGIB.
pearl: High-risk UGIB needs ABC, blood support and endoscopy; history of cirrhosis/varices changes the pre-endoscopy drug bundle.
pivot: Stable low-risk UGIB may allow less urgent endoscopy after validated risk assessment.

steps: Resuscitate
Two large IV accesses, crossmatch, FBC/coagulation and perfusion assessment; transfuse based on symptoms and cardiac context.
Treat suspected ulcer
IV PPI per upper-GI bleed pathway; review NSAIDs/antithrombotics.
Control bleeding
Urgent endoscopy once stabilised; consider interventional radiology/surgery if uncontrolled.
Prevent recurrence
Test/treat H. pylori and review gastroprotective treatment.
management.safety: Avoid excessive crystalloid that delays appropriate red-cell replacement.
management.local: Educational answer; confirm local clinical guidelines, doses and relevant senior-led escalation.

stem: A 64-year-old with smoking history presents with progressive breathlessness and a new moderate unilateral pleural effusion. He is afebrile with no heart-failure signs. Ultrasound confirms free-flowing fluid and a safe drainage pocket.
ask: Which initial diagnostic strategy is MOST appropriate?
options: Give long-term diuretics without fluid analysis because all effusions are transudates.
Arrange ultrasound-guided diagnostic thoracentesis with pleural fluid chemistry, microscopy/culture and cytology as appropriate.
Perform blind high-volume aspiration without ultrasound to save time.
Insert a chest drain for every undiagnosed non-loculated effusion.
Treat empirically for tuberculosis without testing because a unilateral effusion proves TB.
explanations: Unilateral unexplained effusion may be malignant or infectious and needs investigation.
Correct: fluid characterisation with paired serum values directs differential diagnosis.
Ultrasound guidance reduces complications and supports safe sampling.
A drain is not universally necessary for initial diagnostic evaluation.
TB is only one of several causes and confirmation should be pursued.
pearl: Light's criteria distinguish exudates from transudates; unilateral unexplained effusion often warrants diagnostic aspiration.
pivot: A typical bilateral effusion with established decompensated heart failure may first be managed with diuresis if no atypical features.

steps: Assess
ABC, oxygen if required, CXR and thoracic ultrasound, medication/exposure/cancer history.
Sample
Ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration with protein/LDH (paired serum), cell count, pH/glucose when infection considered, microbiology and cytology.
Interpret
Exudate triggers infection, malignancy, inflammatory and PE differential; TB tests where epidemiologically appropriate.
Plan
Symptom drainage when appropriate and referral for persistent/malignant effusion.
management.safety: Pleural pH must be collected/handled correctly when parapneumonic infection is suspected.
management.local: Educational answer; confirm local clinical guidelines, doses and relevant senior-led escalation.

stem: A 50-year-old receiving red-cell transfusion develops abrupt fever 39.4°C, lumbar pain, hypotension and dark urine 15 minutes into the unit. She had been stable before transfusion.
ask: Which is the BEST first response?
options: Slow transfusion rate and reassess temperature after 20 minutes.
Give paracetamol and continue the same unit.
Stop transfusion, maintain IV access with normal saline, summon help and notify blood bank immediately.
Start a new red-cell unit from the same batch without checking identity.
Discharge once back pain improves.
explanations: Possible acute haemolytic transfusion reaction requires stopping blood immediately.
Antipyretics alone cannot prevent ongoing haemolysis and shock.
Correct: stop suspected incompatible blood, support ABC and initiate transfusion-reaction investigation.
Potential mismatched product must be investigated before further transfusion.
Shock and haemoglobinuria can lead to DIC and AKI requiring monitoring.
pearl: Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction commonly presents early with fever, pain, hypotension and dark urine; immediately stop blood.
pivot: Isolated mild urticaria without systemic symptoms may permit a different graded response under transfusion policy.

steps: Stop and check
Stop blood, keep IV access with saline, verify patient/product identity and notify blood bank.
Stabilise
ABCDE, oxygen if needed, manage shock and monitor urine output.
Investigate
Send appropriate pre/post samples, urine, haemolysis markers, coagulation and returned bag/tubing.
Prevent
Document reaction and communicate safe future compatibility requirements.
management.safety: Never resume a suspected severe haemolytic reaction unit.
management.local: Educational answer; confirm local clinical guidelines, doses and relevant senior-led escalation.

stem: A 58-year-old with chronic venous insufficiency has rapid onset of tender, sharply demarcated bright-red erythema on one shin with temperature 38.1°C. No bullae or necrosis, pain is proportionate, BP normal, lactate normal.
ask: What is the BEST initial management?
options: Urgent wide fascial debridement for every sharply bordered erythema.
Treat suspected streptococcal erysipelas with appropriate systemic antibiotics and early clinical reassessment.
Prescribe topical antifungal alone because infection in venous legs is always fungal.
Give oral prednisolone as sole therapy.
Delay therapy until blood cultures turn positive.
explanations: Features fit uncomplicated erysipelas without deep necrotising signs.
Correct: sharply raised demarcation and systemic fever suggest superficial dermal streptococcal infection.
Acute unilateral hot painful erythema with fever requires systemic treatment.
Steroids do not eradicate infection and can worsen untreated cellulitis.
Cultures may be negative; uncomplicated erysipelas is diagnosed clinically.
pearl: Erysipelas is a superficial streptococcal skin infection with sharply defined raised borders; look for portals such as tinea pedis.
pivot: Disproportionate pain, bullae, crepitus or shock suggests deeper necrotising infection requiring immediate surgery.

steps: Assess severity
Vitals and risk factors, borders, abscess, necrosis, immune state and glycaemic control.
Treat
Appropriate narrow-spectrum anti-streptococcal antibiotic adjusted for allergy and severity, limb elevation and analgesia.
Address portal
Treat toe-web fungal disease, oedema/skin breaks; reassess response in 24–48h.
Escalate
Admit for toxicity, progression or failure of oral therapy.
management.safety: Consider DVT or stasis dermatitis if clinical features diverge.
management.local: Educational answer; confirm local clinical guidelines, doses and relevant senior-led escalation.

stem: A 69-year-old experiences 12 minutes of left arm weakness and speech slurring, now completely resolved. BP 150/90 mmHg, irregularly irregular pulse 104/min and glucose normal. He has no headache or prior stroke.
ask: What is the BEST next step?
options: Reassure because complete resolution excludes cerebral ischaemia.
Arrange urgent same-day TIA/stroke assessment with vascular imaging, ECG and risk-directed antithrombotic plan.
Wait for a second attack before neuroimaging.
Start long-term aspirin and warfarin together immediately without brain imaging or AF confirmation.
Order outpatient EEG as the main investigation because transient signs imply seizure.
explanations: TIA is a warning of imminent stroke despite complete symptom resolution.
Correct: expedite aetiology and secondary prevention; atrial fibrillation is a possible cardioembolic source.
Early recurrent stroke risk is highest soon after TIA; waiting is unsafe.
Antithrombotic choice depends on imaging and source; empiric combination carries bleeding risk.
A focal negative neurological deficit with dysarthria suggests vascular event; seizure is differential but not first assumption.
pearl: Resolved focal deficit is a TIA emergency: evaluate rapidly and intervene on stroke mechanisms.
pivot: If MRI shows infarction, the event is tissue-positive stroke even if symptoms have resolved.

steps: Refer rapidly
Urgent specialist TIA/stroke pathway, document onset/duration and neurological findings.
Investigate
Brain and vascular imaging per protocol, ECG for AF, BP, lipids, glucose and carotid disease.
Prevent
Antiplatelet or anticoagulation according to mechanism/timing, statin and risk-factor management.
Counsel
Return immediately for recurrent symptoms; driving and lifestyle guidance.
management.safety: Do not delay referral based solely on a low risk score.
management.local: Educational answer; confirm local clinical guidelines, doses and relevant senior-led escalation.

stem: A 44-year-old notices a changing 9 mm pigmented back lesion with asymmetric borders, colour variegation and a new nodular component. His mother had melanoma. There is no infection or bleeding.
options: Freeze the lesion with liquid nitrogen and reassess appearance.
Perform complete excisional biopsy with narrow clinical margins or urgent specialist referral for appropriate biopsy.
Prescribe topical corticosteroid for four weeks.
Shave a superficial portion only without assessing depth.
Reassure because lesion is under 1 cm.
explanations: Cryotherapy destroys histological architecture and can delay diagnosis.
Correct: changing ABCDE features require histopathologic diagnosis with accurate Breslow staging.
A suspicious melanocytic lesion is not a rash to trial steroids.
Partial superficial sampling may impair Breslow thickness assessment; biopsy choice requires guideline alignment.
Melanoma can be smaller than 6 mm; evolution and atypia matter.
pearl: Evolution, asymmetry, border irregularity and colour variation are high-risk melanoma signs; histology determines staging.
pivot: A stable symmetric uniformly coloured nevus without concerning features may be photographed/monitored under appropriate dermoscopy review.

steps: Assess
ABCDE changes, personal/family history and full skin examination.
Biopsy safely
Excisional biopsy with narrow diagnostic margins when feasible, or dermatology referral for complex sites.
Stage/manage
Histological Breslow thickness and ulceration guide wider excision and sentinel node discussion.
Prevent
Sun protection and skin surveillance for patient/family.
management.safety: Do not destroy suspicious lesions without histology.
management.local: Educational answer; confirm local clinical guidelines, doses and relevant senior-led escalation.

stem: A 73-year-old with benign prostatic hyperplasia has suprapubic discomfort and minimal urine for 18 hours. Creatinine is 220 µmol/L (baseline 95), bladder scan shows 1100 mL, and ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis. He is stable without sepsis.
options: Administer high-dose IV furosemide without relieving obstruction.
Decompress the bladder with appropriate catheterisation and monitor urine output/electrolytes for post-obstructive diuresis.
Start chronic dialysis immediately without relieving the urinary blockage.
Give nitrofurantoin as sole therapy even without infection evidence.
Wait one week for an elective flow study before catheterisation.
explanations: Diuretics do not relieve retention and may worsen electrolyte imbalance.
Correct: mechanical bladder outlet obstruction causes postrenal AKI; drainage and surveillance are essential.
Obstruction is potentially reversible; dialysis depends on emergency indications.
Antibiotics do not relieve mechanical retention.
Prolonged obstruction risks renal damage; urgent decompression is indicated.
pearl: Postrenal AKI may improve after drainage, but brisk post-obstructive diuresis can cause fluid/electrolyte loss.
pivot: In painless chronic retention without renal impairment, urgency and approach may differ but still need urologic assessment.

steps: Relieve
Catheterise safely, assess difficult catheter need and obtain urology help if resistance/trauma.
Monitor
Hourly urine output initially, BP, Na/K/creatinine and fluid balance for post-obstructive diuresis.
Treat cause
Review alpha blockade, prostate evaluation and long-term catheter/operative options.
Safety-net
Look for sepsis, haematuria or failure of creatinine recovery.
management.safety: Avoid repeated traumatic catheter attempts if urethral injury is suspected.
management.local: Educational answer; confirm local clinical guidelines, doses and relevant senior-led escalation.

stem: A 66-year-old taking amiodarone for arrhythmia has three weeks of worsening dry cough and exertional dyspnoea. SpO2 90% room air, no fever and CT chest reveals bilateral patchy interstitial infiltrates. No alternative infection is yet demonstrated.
options: Increase amiodarone dose because breathlessness indicates worsening atrial fibrillation.
Immediately stop or withhold amiodarone with cardiology guidance and evaluate drug-related interstitial lung injury alongside infection.
Give antibiotics alone for three months without checking medication history.
Prescribe inhaled salbutamol alone for presumed asthma.
Reassure that pulmonary toxicity can only occur during the first treatment week.
explanations: Amiodarone can cause pulmonary toxicity and further exposure may worsen lung injury.
Correct: exposure and CT pattern warrant drug toxicity assessment and alternative rhythm management.
Noninfective drug lung toxicity may progress untreated.
Interstitial infiltrates and medication exposure do not suggest reversible bronchospasm as sole issue.
Amiodarone pulmonary toxicity may be delayed and cumulative.
pearl: Amiodarone can cause pneumonitis months/years into therapy; consider medication toxicity in unexplained new infiltrates.
pivot: If infectious findings and microbiology support pneumonia, targeted antibiotic therapy becomes central while evaluating the drug.

steps: Stabilise
Oxygen as needed, ECG and assess severity; involve cardiology and respiratory.
Investigate
Medication duration/dose, chest CT, lung function and infection/autoimmune differential.
Stop exposure
Withhold amiodarone after arrhythmia risk review and choose safer alternate rhythm strategy.
Treat severe disease
Specialist-directed systemic steroids for significant pneumonitis and longitudinal lung monitoring.
management.safety: Drug has long half-life; symptoms may persist despite discontinuation.
management.local: Educational answer; confirm local clinical guidelines, doses and relevant senior-led escalation.

stem: A 63-year-old with metastatic squamous-cell cancer has increasing confusion, constipation and polyuria. Corrected calcium is 3.8 mmol/L, creatinine 180 µmol/L, ECG shows short QT and BP 102/64 mmHg.
ask: Which immediate treatment is MOST appropriate?
options: Give oral calcium supplements for bone support.
Start IV isotonic fluids with careful reassessment, rapid calcitonin when indicated and antiresorptive therapy while treating cause.
Give thiazide diuretic to promote renal calcium loss.
Give only oral vitamin D and observe for three weeks.
Give IV bicarbonate as primary calcium antidote.
explanations: Further calcium worsens hypercalcaemia.
Correct: severe symptomatic malignancy-related hypercalcaemia needs rehydration and rapid/longer-lasting calcium-lowering treatment.
Thiazides reduce urinary calcium excretion and can worsen hypercalcaemia.
Severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia is an emergency and vitamin D may aggravate it.
Bicarbonate does not replace hydration, calcitonin/antiresorptive management.
pearl: Severe hypercalcaemia affects kidneys and brain; hydrate, treat cause and select calcium-lowering agent by renal function.
pivot: Mild incidental stable hypercalcaemia can undergo outpatient endocrine workup.

steps: Stabilise
IV access, ECG, fluid status, mental state, electrolytes, renal function and volume-guided isotonic saline.
Lower calcium
Calcitonin for rapid transient effect and appropriate antiresorptive (bisphosphonate or denosumab) after kidney/oncology review.
Find cause
Malignancy burden, PTH/PTHrP context, drugs and immobility.
Monitor
Calcium, phosphate, magnesium, fluid overload and renal function; plan cancer/palliative care.
management.safety: Avoid unmonitored large fluid volumes in heart failure or advanced renal disease.
management.local: Educational answer; confirm local clinical guidelines, doses and relevant senior-led escalation.
